title: POC Weekly - Latency Tuning (TTFT, Streaming, Kernels)
summary: Weekly POC sync with Crestline Financial to review TTFT benchmarks, streaming stability, sequence-length impacts, and kernel choices. Agreed on next steps: run 1k request throughput test with streaming enabled, iterate kernel profile, and share updated benchmark sheet and config for Dedicated trial.
transcript:
[15:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining, good to see you all. we got about 45 minutes, we'll run through the TTFT numbers and then jordan will talk about kernel tuning, uh and then open for q's.
[15:02] Ethan Ross: yeah thanks maya, quick note — priya and aisha are on the line, we pulled the latest load tests this morning.
[15:03] Priya Sharma: hi, yea we saw the TTFT spike on longer sequences, like when seq len goes above 1,024, latency jumps. not sure if that's kernel switching or kv behavior.
[15:04] Jordan Lee: right, so that matches what we saw; default kernel path was switching to the slower attention implementation at ~1.1k tokens, which adds a ~40-60ms bump per token for subsequent generation, and first-token suffers if streaming handshake isn't optimized.
[15:06] Mark Liu: can you clarify streaming handshake? i thought streaming would reduce TTFT not increase it.
[15:07] Jordan Lee: sure, so streaming reduces downstream client-side wait, but server-side we need to warm the streaming buffer and sometimes do an extra serialize step; if the runtime falls back kernels or does a sync flush, that adds to TTFT. we saw a pattern where non-quantized kernels triggered extra memcpy on our infra.
[15:09] Aisha Khan: we're on k8s with gpus attached via our cloud provider; i think some of the memcpy penalties are showing up across the node boundary.
[15:10] Ben Carter: interesting — any suggestions to avoid that?
[15:11] Jordan Lee: two pragmatic knobs: pin to the fast kernel profile for the expected seq length distribution, and enable continuous streaming mode (reduces handshake overhead). also prefix/KV cache helps a lot for repeated contexts, we saw ~20% TTFT improvement when cache hits were ~60%.
[15:13] Ethan Ross: for our workloads most requests are 1-1.2k tokens on initial prompt, then 200-300 tokens on completions. so the initial token is critical.
[15:14] Maya Patel: thanks — that aligns with a dedicated configuration we recommended. question: did you try the new kernel selection override we pushed last week?
[15:15] Priya Sharma: we tried but saw some instability under burst — sequences would fall back mid-request and we'd get higher p99.
[15:16] Jordan Lee: that's likely due to autoscaling and heterogeneous GPU types. if a request gets routed to a different capacity tier that doesn't have the optimized kernels, fallback happens. we can enforce same-kernel-only routing during the POC to keep baselines stable.
[15:18] Mark Liu: how invasive is that? can we do same-kernel routing without major infra changes?
[15:19] Jordan Lee: yes, on Redwood Dedicated we have routing policies; for Private we can add a placement constraint on the inference daemonset. minimal infra patch — mostly config change.
[15:21] Priya Sharma: what about quantization? we use 8-bit for throughput but worried about quality. did you measure TTFT delta between q8 and fp16?
[15:22] Jordan Lee: q8 cut token compute by ~30% in our tests but increased first-token by ~10ms in some kernels due to reprojection costs. overall p50 improved but p99 depends on fallback behavior and sequence cutover.
[15:24] Ethan Ross: can you share the exact benchmark sheet? we compared to Anthropic numbers and saw different tradeoffs.
[15:25] Maya Patel: we'll share the benchmark spreadsheet and the kernel profile we used. note we also ran a streaming-enabled test and a non-streaming test; results are in tabs.
[15:26] Aisha Khan: one more thing — audit logs and SSO. if we move to Dedicated or Private, we need KMS integration and SOC2 docs. are those available?
[15:27] Maya Patel: yes, we'll attach SOC2 package and KMS integration guide. Jordan, can you call out any additional audit hooks?
[15:28] Jordan Lee: we emit request-level traces and token-level cost breakdowns into the console; on private we can push logs into your SIEM via syslog or cloud collector. RBAC and SAML are supported.
[15:30] Priya Sharma: good. for the next test can we enable streaming with a 40ms flush interval and the kernel override? that should mimic production.
[15:31] Jordan Lee: yes that's doable; we'll also set KV-cache warmers to prime common prefixes. plan: run 1k request burst with 50 concurrent clients, streaming on, record TTFT p50/p95/p99 and CPU/GPU memcpy metrics.
[15:33] Ethan Ross: timeline? we want results before exec review next thursday.
[15:34] Maya Patel: we'll aim to run tests tomorrow and have a results pass by wednesday EOD. if anything fails we'll escalate.
[15:35] Mark Liu: acceptable. also, cost question — if we pin kernels and enforce routing, does that bump cost?
[15:36] Ben Carter: slightly, because you reduce ability to use cheaper inference instances, but you get predictable latency. we'll provide an estimate.
[15:37] Priya Sharma: can we get a tradeoff sheet — predicted cost delta vs latency improvements?
[15:38] Maya Patel: yes, redwood optimize team can generate that; i'll include an approximate delta in the next email.
[15:39] Aisha Khan: one question on streaming reliability — we saw a case where the stream cut out mid-response and client retried causing duplicate completions. can we add idempotency token handling?
[15:40] Jordan Lee: we support request IDs and resumable streams in the SDK; we'll share sample code. also there's a fallback policy to return final tokens if duplicate detected.
[15:41] Ethan Ross: perfect. anything else?
[15:42] Maya Patel: quick recap: run throughput test with streaming + kernel override, share benchmark sheet and SOC2/KMS docs, provide cost-vs-latency tradeoff estimate, share SDK snippets for idempotency. jordan will own the test run, maya will send docs.
[15:44] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone. end of meeting.
